WHY IT HAS TO EXIST

The camera roll is a landfill.
Sorted by nothing.

The average phone carries thousands of photos, research suggests roughly a fifth of them are duplicates and dead shots, and surveys find most people never delete any of it. Everything is saved; nothing is findable.

F·01

The pile only grows

Bursts, screenshots, the same sunset eleven times, WhatsApp re-saves of photos you already have. Storage research puts the junk share of a typical library at around one photo in five, and in one survey most people admitted they never delete duplicates. The pile wins by default, because sorting ten years by hand is a job that does not get done.

F·02

The story is written inside, and ignored

Every camera writes the story into the file: the exact moment, the GPS position, the device, the burst sequence. That's enough to reconstruct the weekend away, the birthday, the site visit, the way you remember them. Most tools use it for one thing: a timeline. The metadata deserves a filing clerk.

F·03

Messengers shred the evidence

WhatsApp and most messengers typically strip the metadata from every photo sent: the when, the where, the camera, gone. Screenshots never had any. Half a modern library ends up dated "unknown", even when the filename is shouting the date out loud. Popular organisers file these as mystery files; the answer is sitting in the name and the folder around them.

F·04

The cloud reads your photos

Free unlimited photo storage ended in 2021; two terabytes now runs about a hundred euros a year, forever. And the scanner comes with the deal: one documented case saw a father's entire Google account permanently destroyed over a toddler's medical photo; police cleared him, the account stayed dead. Google separately paid $100M to settle claims over face-grouping photos without consent. Your family archive should not live inside someone else's risk model.

WHO IT SERVES

Built for everyone
with a decade in their pocket.

Our own archives first

The VF network produces images all day, every day: property documentation across the German operation, product renders off the forge, years of family and company history across three countries. It all lands on our own storage, and it's the mess SnapIT is built to file. It proves itself the VF way, on our own drives first. If it can't turn our ten-year pile into a clean archive, it doesn't ship.

NAS · OWN METALMT · DE · UKFILED IN THE OPEN

Families

The christening, the moves, the grandparents' folders copied off old laptops: decades scattered across devices and duplicated in every direction. SnapIT folds it into one archive, one timeline of events, with the duplicates gone and nothing lost.

Creators & builders

Screenshots, renders, references and exports breed faster than holiday photos and rot faster too. SnapIT uses camera and source metadata to split the work library from the life library automatically, and keeps both filed.

Property & business records

Handover photos, meter readings, damage documentation, receipts: photos that are documents, where the embedded timestamp and place are the whole point. SnapIT files them as evidence: by property, by date, findable in seconds years later.

Cloud leavers

The takeout ZIP from a cloud photo service is a famous mess: mangled folders, sidecar files, stripped structure. SnapIT is built to receive that dump, reassemble the story from what survived, and give your library a home you own.

WHAT IT CHANGES

From ten thousand files
to a filed archive.

The measure of a photo organiser is whether you can find the photo you're thinking of in ten seconds, ten years later. We judge SnapIT on the finding.

Filed like a human would.

SnapIT clusters photos by time, place and camera into events: the weekend it was. Duplicates and burst near-copies fold into one keeper; screenshots get their own lane instead of polluting the memories.

Read, then repaired.

Photos with stripped metadata get their story back, inferred from filename patterns, folder context and the photos around them. SnapIT marks every repaired field as inferred and never invents one silently.

Yours, on your metal.

Everything runs locally: your NAS, your desktop, your drive. No corporate scanner reads your family, no subscription meters your memories, and the output is a plain, portable folder tree no tool can hold hostage.

THE MECHANICS

Four layers,
one archive.

Built the VF way: deterministic filing driven by the file's own evidence, inference marked as inference, and an output any other tool can read. SnapIT organises your library and never takes it hostage. Like every VF system, it leaves the lab with the engine fitted and the harness tuned.

LAYER 1

The reader

Every byte of embedded story extracted: capture moment, GPS position, camera and lens, burst sequence, edit history. The standard metadata that every camera writes and most software throws a timeline at.

LAYER 2

The repair bench

Stripped and mystery files get their story reconstructed: dates parsed from messenger filenames, places inferred from the folder and the photos taken around the same moment. Every repaired field carries an "inferred" mark, so the archive never lies about what it knows.

LAYER 3

The clustering

SnapIT folds the library into events by time and place; perceptual matching folds duplicates, re-saves and burst shots into a single keeper with the rest tucked behind it. Screenshots, documents and work images are recognised and routed to their own lanes.

LAYER 4

The archive

The output is a clean, human-named folder tree and album set on your own storage, readable by any viewer, portable to any tool, backed up like the files they are. Your library leaves better than SnapIT found it.

QUESTIONS

Asked.
Answered.

Which platforms does SnapIT run on today?

R·02a is live now with a Linux .deb and a Windows .exe. A signed macOS build (universal binary with Developer ID notarisation) arrives with R·02b, together with event clustering, plain-language search and an auto-updater. SnapIT is desktop-first with a mobile companion, and it stores the library on your disk, your NAS or your S3-compatible bucket.

Does SnapIT upload my photos anywhere?

No. Everything runs locally on your NAS, your desktop or your drive. No corporate scanner reads your family, no subscription meters your memories, and the licence never phones home. The output is a plain, portable folder tree and album set that any viewer can read and any tool can import, so nothing holds your library hostage.

What does SnapIT do with photos that lost their metadata?

Messengers strip the when, the where and the camera from most photos they send, and screenshots never had any. SnapIT's repair bench reconstructs the story: dates parsed from messenger filename patterns, places inferred from the folder and the photos taken around the same moment. Every repaired field carries an inferred mark, so the archive never lies about what it knows.

How does SnapIT handle duplicates, bursts and screenshots?

SnapIT clusters the library into events by time, place and camera. Perceptual matching folds duplicates, WhatsApp re-saves and burst shots into a single keeper with the rest tucked behind it, so the duplicates go and nothing is lost. Screenshots, documents and work images are recognised and routed to their own lanes instead of polluting the memories.

How much does SnapIT cost?

SnapIT is a one-off perpetual licence with no renewals. Personal is €59 for the first 500 buyers (€89 standard). The Family Pack is €99 founding (€149 standard) for five profiles with per-profile PIN and a shared library. Pro / Studio is €199 founding (€249 standard) for commercial use. Upgrades are optional at €29 per major version; minor updates are free forever.

Can I read the SnapIT source?

Yes. The desktop source is public at github.com/vfempire-hq/snapit-desktop under the FSL-1.1-ALv2 licence. The licence pair is Ed25519-signed and verified offline, household profiles use Argon2id-hashed PINs, and the catalogue scan runs across any folder or NAS mount. Founding pricing from €59 is live today on Linux and Windows.
